title: Albania and Armenia achieve hepatitis B control milestone, strengthening the WHO European Region’s path to elimination - World Health Organization (WHO)

analysis.time: The milestone was achieved in 2026, with the validation ceremony held on 6 October 2026. The publication date is 12 October 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Albania and Armenia, with a focus on children aged 6–8 years.
analysis.event: Albania and Armenia achieved hepatitis B control targets, validated by the European Technical Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (ETAGE) following an assessment of country reports and recommendations from the ETAGE Working Group on Hepatitis B at its sixth meeting on 10 April 2026.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Country serosurveys showed that more than 20 years of sustained hepatitis B vaccination led to the elimination of hepatitis B among children aged 6–8 years, with no children testing positive for the hepatitis B virus surface antigen, corresponding to an estimated prevalence of 0%. Hepatitis B can cause lifelong infection and serious complications, including cirrhosis and liver cancer.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The achievement was validated by ETAGE, and a certificate of validation was handed over to the Armenian Minister of Health. The milestone is part of the WHO European Region’s efforts to eliminate hepatitis B.

analysis.brief_en: Albania and Armenia have achieved hepatitis B control targets, marking a significant milestone in the WHO European Region’s efforts to eliminate the virus. This accomplishment was validated by the European Technical Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (ETAGE) following an assessment of country reports and recommendations from the ETAGE Working Group on Hepatitis B at its sixth meeting on 10 April 2026. Country serosurveys revealed that over 20 years of sustained vaccination efforts have led to the elimination of hepatitis B among children aged 6–8 years, with no positive cases detected. The validation ceremony took place on 6 October 2026, where the certificate was handed over to the Armenian Minister of Health. Hepatitis B can cause lifelong infection and serious complications such as cirrhosis and liver cancer, making early prevention critical. This achievement joins other countries in the WHO European Region that have already met similar targets, highlighting progress in public health initiatives.

title: Tislelizumab-induced immune-mediated hepatotoxicity combined with two episodes of hepatitis B virus reactivation: a case report - Frontiers

analysis.location_and_population: A 61-year-old man with lung squamous cell carcinoma in China.
analysis.event: A patient developed immune-mediated hepatotoxicity (IMH) and hepatitis B virus reactivation (HBVr) simultaneously after receiving tislelumab, leading to a delay in IMH treatment and a dilemma in treatment strategy.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Two episodes of HBVr occurred, with liver function tests showing significant abnormalities. The patient experienced a delay in IMH treatment and a dilemma in continuing glucocorticoid (GC) therapy or stopping it.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The case required a multidisciplinary approach, close monitoring of liver function and HBV-DNA, and a carefully balanced treatment strategy combining GCs with intensified antiviral therapy. The coexistence of HBVr and IMH in the same patient presented challenges to diagnosis and treatment.

analysis.brief_en: A 61-year-old man with lung squamous cell carcinoma developed immune-mediated hepatotoxicity (IMH) and hepatitis B virus reactivation (HBVr) after receiving tislelumab. The coexistence of these conditions led to a delay in IMH treatment and a dilemma in treatment strategy. The case required a multidisciplinary approach and careful management to balance antiviral and immunosuppressive therapies.
analysis.summary_en: A 61-year-old man with lung squamous cell carcinoma developed immune-mediated hepatotoxicity (IMH) and hepatitis B virus reactivation (HBVr) after receiving tislelumab. The coexistence of these conditions led to a delay in IMH treatment and a dilemma in treatment strategy. The case required a multidisciplinary approach and careful management to balance antiviral and immunosuppressive therapies.

title: Hepatitis B Vaccine Response Holds Steady in Children with G6PD Deficiency, Study Finds - Bioengineer.org

analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-10-12. Event date: March 2024 to January 2025. The study measured antibody durability over two and a half years on average.
analysis.location_and_population: Heyuan, in China’s Guangdong province. The study involved 505 children, of whom 55 had G6PD deficiency and 450 were healthy controls. The population included children aged 1 to 4 years.
analysis.event: A study found that the hepatitis B vaccine response is stable in children with G6PD deficiency. The research was conducted by Zhiqiang Ou and colleagues at the Guangdong Institute of Biological Products and Drugs and several Chinese public health institutions. The findings are based on antibody persistence measurements and are described as reassuring but not definitive.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study involved 505 children, with 55 having G6PD deficiency. Seroprotection was observed in 87.0% of G6PD-deficient children and 82.2% of controls. The risk difference was 4.8 percentage points, but the confidence interval included the null value, indicating no significant difference. The study does not address vaccine safety directly.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is ongoing and has limitations, including the inability to distinguish among G6PD genotypes and detect rare adverse events. The authors emphasize that their design cannot definitively settle questions of vaccine safety in this population.

analysis.brief_en: A study published on October 12, 2026, by Bioengineer.org found that the hepatitis B vaccine response remains stable in children with G6PD deficiency. Conducted in Heyuan, Guangdong province, China, the research involved 505 children, including 55 with confirmed G6PD deficiency and 450 healthy controls. The study measured antibody persistence six months after the third hepatitis B vaccine dose, with a mean interval of 30 months. Seroprotection, defined as anti-HBs levels of at least 10 mIU/mL, was observed in 87.0% of G6PD-deficient children and 82.2% of controls. The risk difference was 4.8 percentage points, but the confidence interval included the null value, suggesting no significant difference. The authors caution that their design cannot definitively address vaccine safety concerns in this population. The findings offer reassurance to families in regions where G6PD deficiency is common, but further studies are needed to explore genotype variations and rare adverse events.
